To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
visual jitter is a visual motion aftereffect that is mediated by extrastriate visual motion areas.

(1) the visual jitter is an adaptation phenomenon that is (2) monocular, (3) has directional selectivity and spatial frequency selectiveness like the motion aftereffect, (4) is transferable across the vertical meridians and has a preferred stimulus size, suggesting (5) involvement of the motion area MT in motion-based compensation of small eye movements.

visual jitter, a phenomenon in which the observer's own small eye movements are mirrored on a static visual display, has the properties of a motion aftereffect and is likely to involve a motion-based compensation of the retinal slip due in part to eye movements, which is mediated by the extrastriate visual motion system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the visual mechanisms of motion-based compensation of the retinal slip due small eye movements, which is a fundamental visual process in the visual system.
how we compensate for the retinal slip that is produced by the eye's own motion, and how we perceive the motion of the external world.
the psychophysics of visual-motion-based compensation and with its underlying neural mechanisms, and it provides new insights into the neural mechanisms for the visual motion system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
visual jitter is a motion-based compensatory mechanism for the retinal slip due mainly to small eye movements.
visual jitter is an extrastriate, monocular motion-based phenomenon that compensates for small eye movements.
the motion after-effect is the first stage in a hierarchy of adaptation processes that includes visual jitter as the second stage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the visual jitter is the result of a motion compensation process, and that the motion compensation process is mediated by a motion-sensitive mechanism in the parietal cortex.

the motion-based compensation of the retinal slip due small eye movements is mediated by the motion after-effect mechanism, but the compensation mechanism is not identical to the motion after-effect itself.
visual jitter is a motion-based compensation of the retinal slip due mainly to small eye movements.
The main takeaway from our work is that

motion after-effect and visual jitter share a common underlying mechanism that is likely to reside in the motion pathway, and the latter effect can be used to psychophysically probe the properties of this motion pathway.
the visual motion system is capable of compensating for retinal slip due even to small eye movements and that this compensation is mediated at the level of extrastriate visual cortex.
the brain can estimate and compensate for the retinal motion due to eye movements by using visual motion information.
